revise.summary: I revised content/lessons/08-tdd.md and both gates pass: the lint prints no ERROR lines at 2,832 words, and the vitest run passes 14 tests. Every high and medium finding is fixed. I checked each fix against the installed 1.3.1 SKILL.md files, the Matt transcripts that exist under /Users/siddharth/Developer/trying/.handoff/transcripts, GitHub Discussion #1136 (read through the gh API, read-only), and the repo: PR #4, PR #7, route.test.ts, setup-env.ts, ADR 0003, the redesign spec and ticket 02, and d21fc2c:06-tdd.md / 07-code-review.md. Changes to the body: tautological tests are now taught correctly; the seam table and chat Scene now use the real public postComment function; the second slice of the worked example is now part of what you asked for; both Scenes now respect the agree-a-seam-first rule. The Try block now tests the Skill instead of the prompt, the Warshoow and audio examples now match their sources, and terms like status code, ADR, Neon branch, fake, browser test and Built-in command are explained at first use. In the questions, I rewrote 5 Final test questions and both seam/tautology Checkpoints. Three questions got new ids (skipped-seam, rename-breaks-test, scenario-best-fit). Right answers are now spread a2 b2 c3 d3 across the Final test. To stay under the word limit, I cut the Pragmatic Programmer quote, the Reddit bullet, two Matt-habit bullets, the SDK-style mocking habit, a Common-mistakes bullet and a cheat-sheet row. The Site story now uses only facts the repo holds.

The X-280 and MAX_BODY examples are now described as copying a number from the code: they check a number, not a behaviour, pass even if nothing enforces the limit, and break on a rename. The code comment is updated to match (tdd/SKILL.md:31; LlgiOCmFG_w.ar 5:24-6:20).

declined.problem: quiz low 7: in scenario-clock, replace 'wait 31 days' with 'Nothing: use the real clock and today's date'.
declined.reason: The suggested replacement would create a second defensible answer: a test can use the real clock and simply create a task whose finished date is 31 days in the past, without faking anything. I kept the original option. It is a weak distractor but unambiguous, and Matt uses the same 'don't literally wait' framing for fake clocks (3MP8D-mdheA 4:28-4:38).

quiz.where: "Fake only at the edges": Checkpoint what-to-fake, "What should the test fake?" (line 180), and Final test scenario-clock, "What should the test fake?" (line 322)
quiz.problem: The Checkpoint and the Final test question are near-duplicates. Both stems end with the same question, and both offer the same four kinds of option: your own module, an internal helper or the database, doing it for real, and the outside boundary. In both, the right answer is the only option that says "passed in", so a Visitor who did the Checkpoint can answer scenario-clock just by matching that phrase. scenario-clock's distractors are also weak: "wait 31 days" is silly, and "The database, always" gives itself away with an absolute.
quiz.evidence: Line 186: "- [x] The SMS service, passed into sign-up as a dependency." Line 330: "- [x] The clock, passed in so the test can set \"today\"." Line 326: "Nothing: create a task and wait 31 days." Line 328: "The database, always, so that the test runs a lot faster." The writing guide's Questions section says: "Don't reuse a Checkpoint as a Final test question." Its pilot review lessons say: "no Checkpoint duplicates a Final test question." mocking.md:3-14 has the "Mock at system boundaries" list and the "Don't mock" list.
quiz.fix:
Keep scenario-clock, since it checks the "may fake" half of goal 3. Point the Checkpoint at the "never fake" column instead:

```checkpoint what-to-fake
Your gym app's sign-up charges the first month and sends a welcome text through an outside SMS service. Four tests each swap one thing for a fake. Which swap breaks the Skill's rule?
- [ ] The SMS service, handed to sign-up as a dependency.
  > That's a boundary you don't control, and you don't want real texts going out on every run. Faking it is the rule working.
- [ ] The payment service that charges the first month.
  > An outside payment service is a system boundary. Faking it is allowed.
- [x] The app's own module that sets the monthly fee.
  > Right. That's your own code. Fake it and the test only checks the fake; let it run for real.
- [ ] The random generator that picks each welcome code.
  > Randomness is a boundary too. A fake makes the result predictable enough to check.
```

In scenario-clock, replace option c with "- [ ] The database, so the test needn't set one up." and this feedback: "> A real test database is preferred where you can have one. The database isn't what makes 31 days hard; time is."

quiz.where: "Seams: agree where tests go first": Checkpoint skipped-seam, option c "Listing every test it plans to write first." and its feedback "A list up front leads to a batch." (lines 100-101)
quiz.problem: The feedback teaches a rule that neither the Skill nor its docs contain, and it contradicts the Lesson's own Try it step 5. There the reader is told to hand the agent a list of cases up front. Option d ("Planning its refactor step") is weak, because the section just before it says there is no refactor step. Option b is ruled out by the stem itself ("already run and failing"). The right option also echoes the section heading almost word for word ("Agreeing with you where the tests go" vs "agree where tests go first").
quiz.evidence: tdd SKILL.md:22-24 (1.3.1) asks only that the seams be written down, confirmed and given a catches/misses note. It says nothing about test lists. docs/engineering/tdd.md:33 warns against tests *written* in bulk, not against a plan of cases. Lesson line 252 (Try it step 5): "If it asks what to cover, offer: empty text takes 1 minute, 201 words take 2, 200 words take 1."
quiz.fix:
Replace the options, keeping the right answer in position a:
- [x] Getting your OK on which boundary to test.
  > Right. No test is written at a seam you haven't agreed. Press Esc and ask for its proposed seams, with what each catches and misses.
- [ ] Writing the code before the test.
  > Test first is the loop working. The problem is the step before it.
- [ ] Writing two or three tests before running any.
  > That would be the start of a batch. One test, run and seen red, is the loop working; what it missed comes before any test.
- [ ] Checking the runner with a test that passes.
  > A test you've only seen pass proves nothing. Starting red is right; the missing step comes before any test.

quiz.where: "Good tests and the three bad ones": Checkpoint rename-breaks-test, "What kind of bad test is it?" (line 152)
quiz.problem: The stem calls it a bad test, so option b ("Nothing's wrong: the test caught a real change.") rules itself out before the reader thinks. Option a ("Tautological: it recomputes what `scale` returns") has nothing in the stem to hang on, since the test checks a call count, not a returned value. That leaves only c and d as live choices, and the right one echoes the body's defining phrase ("checks how the code works instead of what it does", line 134).
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 152 ends "What kind of bad test is it?". Line 155 is option b, "Nothing's wrong: the test caught a real change.". tests.md:38-45 lists the red flags, including "Asserting on call counts/order". The natural misconception, updating the test to count the new helpers, is never offered.
quiz.fix:
Change the last sentence of the stem to "What's the right verdict on this test?". Then replace options a and b:
- [ ] A good catch: update it to count calls to both new helpers.
  > Every recipe still scales correctly, so nothing broke. Counting the new helpers ties the test even tighter to the inside of `scale`.
- [ ] Too broad: replace it with one test per helper.
  > The helpers are internals, not the interface. Tests per helper break on the next split too.
Keep c (horizontal slicing) and d (right) as they are.

quiz.where: Final test spot-tautological, options a "It should fake `shippingCost` so it runs faster." and d "It's horizontal slicing, because it covers one parcel." (lines 372, 378)
quiz.problem: Two of the three distractors are not real misconceptions. Faking the function under test so it runs faster is absurd. "Horizontal slicing because it covers one parcel" gives a reason that has nothing to do with the term. The reader is left choosing between b and c.
quiz.evidence: Writing guide, Questions: "Distractors are real misconceptions." Lesson line 136 defines horizontal slicing as "Every test first, then all the code", which no reader would connect to "covers one parcel". mocking.md:10-14 says not to mock your own modules, so a believable wrong option is the reverse belief: that it should use a mock.
quiz.fix:
Replace a and d with:
- [ ] It calls the real `shippingCost` instead of a mock.
  > `shippingCost` is the code under test. Calling it for real through its interface is right; mocks are for boundaries.
- [ ] It should cover every parcel weight, not just one.
  > More weights checked the same way would all share the flaw. One case per test is fine; the problem is the expected value.
The right option, c, stays the same length or shorter than the others.

quiz.where: Final test spot-batch, "Asked to build a password-strength checker with `/tdd`, the agent creates a file of 15 tests and runs them" (line 395)
quiz.problem: The stem arguably holds a second mistake. The agent's first visible action is writing tests, with no seam agreed. The skipped-seam Checkpoint taught readers to spot exactly that. No option names it, so the key stays unique, but a spot- question should hold exactly one mistake.
quiz.evidence: Checkpoint skipped-seam (line 95) treats "The agent's first reply is a new test file" as having skipped seam agreement. tdd SKILL.md:22 says "No test is written at an unconfirmed seam."
quiz.fix: Change the stem to: "Asked to build a password-strength checker with `/tdd`, the agent agrees the seam with you, then creates a file of 15 tests and runs them: all 15 fail. Then it writes the whole checker, and all 15 pass. Spot the mistake."

quiz.where: Final test why-test-first, right option "Tests written afterwards fit the code, not what it should do." (line 422)
quiz.problem: The right answer is as absolute as option d, which its own feedback rejects as "Too strong" because tests written afterwards "can catch some bugs". A sharp reader can argue that b over-claims in the same way.
quiz.evidence: Line 427, d's feedback: "Too strong. They can catch some bugs, but nobody saw them fail...". Body line 24 makes a hedged claim: "the tests described that code, gaps included".
quiz.fix: Change option b to: "Tests written afterwards can bend to fit the code, gaps and all." At 66 characters it is still shorter than d (71).

quiz.where: Final test sequence-loop, option a "Agree the seam → one failing test → just enough code → refactor → next test" (line 408)
quiz.problem: No Final test option depends on goal 1's clause "then only the code that makes it pass". Every sequence option except b already says "just enough code". The refactor point option a tests is already the subject of scenario-no-refactor. Because a is just d plus one step, d is also easy to find by convergence.
quiz.evidence: Goal 1 (line 14): "write one failing test, then only the code that makes it pass". tdd SKILL.md:36: "Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features." scenario-no-refactor (line 334) already tests that there is no refactor step.
quiz.fix:
Replace option a with:
- [ ] Agree the seam → one failing test → code for the next tests too → next test
  > Green means only enough code for this test. Code for tests that don't exist yet is speculative, and nothing has shown it's needed.

quiz.where: Final test spot-side-channel, option c feedback "\"yoga\" is an independent literal." (line 389)
quiz.problem: The feedback doesn't answer the option. The stem's query only checks "a row exists"; it never checks the value "yoga". The option's claim "it checks a value it just set" is wrong because `bookClass` wrote the row, not the test.
quiz.evidence: Line 383 stem: "runs its own query on the bookings table to check a row exists." Line 388: "It's tautological, because it checks a value it just set."
quiz.fix: Change the feedback to: "> The test didn't write that row; `bookClass` did, so nothing is restated from the code. The problem is the route the test takes to check it."

quiz.where: Final test scenario-tickets, "You've grilled a feature, written a spec with `/to-spec` and split it into four tickets with `/to-tickets`." (line 347)
quiz.problem: `/to-tickets` appears nowhere in the Lesson outside this stem, and "grilled" is never explained in this Lesson; line 199 only links to Grilling. A cold reader meets both first in the Final test.
quiz.evidence: grep for "to-tickets" in content/lessons/08-tdd.md finds only line 347. grep for "grill" finds only line 199 (a table row with a link) and line 347.
quiz.fix: Change the stem to: "You've talked a feature through, written a spec with `/to-spec`, and had `/to-tickets` split it into four tickets. What do you type to build the first ticket?"

reader.where: ## The idea: red, then green, one slice at a time, terminal Scene, first caption: "# The seam is already agreed: the comments route (more on seams below)." (line 46)
reader.problem: This is the first place a cold reader meets "seam" and "route" (the goals only list them). Neither is explained here: "seam" is defined at line 81 and "route handler" at line 85. A forward pointer like "(more on seams below)" is not the in-place clause the guide asks for, so the reader watches the first Scene without knowing what was agreed.
reader.evidence: Line 46 is the first body use of both words. Line 81: "The Skill calls the place you test at a **seam**: the public boundary...". Line 85: "Its route handler (the function that runs when the comment box sends a new Comment...)". Writing guide, Voice: "Explain every term at or before first use, in a clause, not a footnote."
reader.fix: Replace line 46 with: "# You and the agent have already agreed where the test plugs in (a seam; more on those below): the comments route, the code that runs when a new Comment arrives. The agent writes one test for the length limit and runs it before writing the check."

reader.where: ## Good tests and the three bad ones: "Its expected values, 2000 and 2001, are typed into the test from the spec, not read out of the code." (line 130), and the code comment "// Tautological: copies a number from the code instead of testing the API" (line 141)
reader.problem: In this site's test, 2000 and 2001 are inputs (body lengths), not expected values. The expected values are 201, 400 and the error message. The Lesson mislabels them in the very section that teaches tautology, which is all about where expected values come from. Then line 141 calls a test with the same literal 2000 bad because it "copies a number from the code". The reader can't see any difference between the two 2000s. The real difference, given at line 149, is that one test checks behaviour and the other doesn't.
reader.evidence: src/app/api/comments/route.test.ts:39-43: `test("a body of exactly 2000 characters is fine, 2001 is rejected"` with `post({ lesson: LESSON, body: "x".repeat(2000) })).status).toBe(201)`, then `"x".repeat(2001)` and an expected 400 plus `{ error: "Comment must be 2000 characters or fewer." }`. tdd/SKILL.md:31: "Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec." Lesson line 262 does use the term correctly: "expected values are plain numbers like 2".
reader.fix: Line 130, second and third sentences: "Its inputs (2000 and 2001 characters) and what it expects back (saved with 201, rejected with 400) all come from the spec, not from the code." Line 141: "// Tautological: restates the code's own constant, so it agrees with the code whatever the API does".

reader.where: ## Good tests and the three bad ones, Implementation-coupled bullet: "The tell: ==it breaks when you rename something, though nothing a user sees has changed.==" (line 134), and Tautological bullet: "...and breaks when someone renames the constant." (line 135)
reader.problem: The Skill's tell is "breaks when you refactor". The Lesson narrows it to "rename", then gives the tautological constant test exactly that symptom one line later. A reader who applies the tells as taught would label the opening story's test both implementation-coupled and tautological, and goal 3 asks them to tell these apart. The narrowed tell also doesn't fit the Checkpoint that follows: there the agent splits `scale` into helpers. That is a restructure, not a rename.
reader.evidence: tdd/SKILL.md:30: "The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed." Lesson line 135: "That passes even if nothing enforces the limit, and breaks when someone renames the constant." Lesson line 152 (Checkpoint rename-breaks-test): "the agent splits the inside of `scale(recipe, servings)` into two smaller helpers".
reader.fix: Line 134: "The tell: ==it breaks when you restructure the code, though nothing a user sees has changed.==" Line 135: end the sentence at "That passes even if nothing enforces the limit." and drop the rename clause.

reader.where: ## When to reach for it: "The fifth row is your call: the Skill decides where seams go, not whether a change deserves the loop" (line 205)
reader.problem: This contradicts the Lesson's central rule. Everywhere else the reader is told that they agree the seams: the agent proposes and waits for an OK, and "You pick the seam. That's a decision for you, not a detail." Saying "the Skill decides where seams go" tells a cold reader the opposite, right where they are deciding when to use the Skill.
reader.evidence: tdd/SKILL.md:22: "Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user." Lesson line 83: "no test is written at a seam you haven't agreed". Line 116: "You pick the seam. That's a decision for you, not a detail." The phrase comes from issue #746's title: `gh issue view 746 --repo mattpocock/skills` returns "tdd: nothing decides whether a change warrants the loop — only where the seams go", CLOSED, NOT_PLANNED.
reader.fix: "The fifth row is your call: the Skill has rules for where tests go, but nothing in it decides whether a change deserves the loop at all (issue #746 asked for that and was closed as not planned)."

reader.where: ## When to reach for it, table row: "`/grill-with-docs` first (see [Grilling](/learn/grilling)), then `/to-spec`" (line 199); Final test scenario-tickets: "You've grilled a feature, written a spec..." (line 347)
reader.problem: This Lesson never says what `/grill-with-docs` does or what "grilling" means. A cold reader is told to reach for an unexplained Skill, and the Final test prompt then assumes they know what it means to have "grilled a feature". Every other new Skill name in the table carries a clause (spec, tickets) or is taught in the Lesson.
reader.evidence: `grep -n -i grill content/lessons/08-tdd.md` finds only line 145 (a Slug in code), line 199 (no clause) and line 347. The Grilling Lesson defines it (04-grilling.md:103), but the writing guide says "a reader landing here cold should still follow." Compare 09-implement.md:24: "grilled you about a comment box (asked question after question until the plan was settled...)".
reader.fix: Line 199: "| You're not sure yet what should happen | `/grill-with-docs` first, where the agent interviews you until the plan is settled (see [Grilling](/learn/grilling)), then `/to-spec` |". Line 347: "You've settled a feature with `/grill-with-docs`, written a spec with `/to-spec` and split it into four tickets with `/to-tickets`."

reader.where: ## Try it yourself, step 2: "If `tdd` is in the list that pops up, delete what you typed. If it isn't, type `/exit`, install Matt's Skills, then run `claude` again:" (line 239)
reader.problem: Only the "found" branch tells the reader to clear the box. In the "not found" branch, `/tdd` is still in the prompt box, so a literal-minded beginner who types `/exit` sends `/tdd/exit`. That is the same append trap the reviser fixed for the other branch. The colon after "run `claude` again" also makes the install block look like the "run claude again" step, so it's unclear where to type the install command.
reader.evidence: Line 239: the delete instruction appears only in the first conditional. Line 242 (the install command) follows "then run `claude` again:".
reader.fix: "2. Type a slash and then tdd, but don't press Enter. If `tdd` is in the list that pops up, delete what you typed and go on to step 3. If it isn't, delete what you typed, type `/exit`, run this install command in the terminal, then run `claude` again:"

reader.where: Several sections: "the functions it exports" (line 81), "not on every edge case" (line 83), "no links in v1" (lines 108, 113), "only showed up in production" (line 174), "(tests and type checks)" (line 217), "the constant for X's post limit equals 280" (line 135)
reader.problem: These are developer terms a Visitor who has never coded won't know, and none comes with a clause.
reader.evidence: The text of each line as quoted. None of these terms is defined anywhere in the Lesson.
reader.fix: "mostly the functions it offers the rest of the code"; "not on every rare, unusual input"; "no links in the first version" (and "in the first version" in the Scene prompt); "only showed up on the live site"; "(tests, and checks that every value has the right type)"; "the post limit on X (formerly Twitter) equals 280".

reader.where: ## Why it matters: "an agent working in layers writes the whole implementation, then the whole layer of tests below it, and tends to cheat at the tests" (line 24)
reader.problem: "Working in layers" and "the whole layer of tests below it" give a cold reader no picture: what is a layer, and why is it "below"? This is the Lesson's opening statement of the problem, so the reader should grasp it at once.
reader.evidence: Line 24 as quoted. The research note (tdd.md line 67) and the earlier source review put Matt's point simply: the agent works in layers, all the code and then all the tests, and tries to cheat at the tests.
reader.fix: "In an April 2026 workshop Matt described the habit: left alone, an agent builds in layers, all of the code first and then all of the tests, and it tends to cheat at the tests."

reader.where: ## A session, step by step: "It runs inside the site's repo, its project folder tracked with Git (a tool that records every change), so the agent reads `GLOSSARY.md`" (line 108)
reader.problem: The "so" makes Git the reason the agent reads the glossary. The real reason is the Skill's instruction to read `GLOSSARY.md` if it exists. A reader could conclude that any Git folder makes the agent read a glossary, or that a repo without one is a problem.
reader.evidence: tdd/SKILL.md:10: "When exploring the codebase, read `GLOSSARY.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language".
reader.fix: "It runs inside the site's repo, its project folder tracked with Git (a tool that records every change). The Skill tells the agent to read the repo's `GLOSSARY.md`, the project's list of agreed terms, if there is one, so it uses words like Comment in test names."

reader.where: ## Common mistakes: "Expecting `tdd` to know about other tickets. It sees the one you give it. Pass the spec too if a slice depends on its neighbours." (line 273)
reader.problem: The Lesson defined a "slice" as one red-green cycle (line 40: "Each cycle is a **vertical slice**"). Here "slice" suddenly means a ticket, and "its neighbours" means the other tickets. A cold reader can't tell which is meant.
reader.evidence: Line 40 defines a slice as one behaviour, one test, one small piece of code. Line 273 uses it for a ticket in the same breath as "other tickets".
reader.fix: "It sees the one you give it. Pass the spec too if this ticket depends on the others."

reader.where: ## Final test, scenario-no-refactor, right-answer feedback: "a separate review with a fresh context does it better." (line 339)
reader.problem: The body says review flags what to tidy (line 42: "flag what to fix"; line 305: "review flags what to tidy"), and the sources say code-review only reports and doesn't edit. Saying review "does it" tells the reader the tidying happens by itself, so they may never act on the findings.
